panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of the patient's right flank showing a clearly visible area of bruising/ecchymosis, a specific cutaneous hemorrhagic manifestation listed in the CCHF vocabulary and supported by the panel-specific caption. The article title is disease-focused on CCHF (with dengue and COVID-19 co-infection), and the caption supplies a concrete captioned manifestation, satisfying the attribution requirement. Confidence is reduced because the patient has a triple co-infection (dengue fever and COVID-19 also present), so the bruise cannot be unambiguously ascribed to CCHF alone; no patient demographics or ethnicity are stated in the caption or in-text mentions.

in_text_mentions: f symptoms was 5.1 + 3.4 days (range 2–12 days). The median duration between the onset of symptoms and hospital admission was 5.1 + 3.1 days (range 2–12 days). All case-patients had sought care for fever and exanthema with a mean duration of 5.2 + 1.64 days (Figure 2). Eight patients had muscle soreness; 4 patients had diarrhea, and 4 had vomiting, nausea, or both. Three case-patients (5, 6, and 9) underwent bone marrow biopsy; 2 of them, patients 5 and 9, had hemophagocytosis, which fulfilled the criteria for hemophagocytic syndrome (Figure 3). Ferritin serum level was elevated in 7 patients.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A is a Wright-stained bone marrow aspiration smear from the CCHF case series (article title 'Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever in Turkey'), showing a macrophage that has phagocytosed an erythrocyte and nuclear remnants (green arrow). Hemophagocytosis in bone marrow was documented in 7 of 14 patients, including confirmed CCHF cases, so the finding is a real patient manifestation attributed to the disease-focused cohort; however, hemophagocytosis is a less common (variant) and non-specific marrow finding, and no matching finding_key exists in the vocabulary (liver histology keys do not apply), hence moderate confidence. B: Panel B is a Wright-stained bone marrow aspiration smear from the same CCHF case series, showing a macrophage with phagocytosed platelets (green arrow). The caption and in-text mention (Figure 3) link hemophagocytosis to the CCHF patient cohort, supporting disease attribution from the disease-focused article title plus...

in_text_mentions: ed disseminated intravascular coagulation. Fibrinogen and D-dimer levels were normal in other patients. Creatine phosphokinase (CPK) levels were elevated in 14 of 19 patients (median 568 U/L, range 81–2,500 U/L). Blood urea nitrogen and creatinine (median 0.8 mg/dL, range 0.5–6.2 mg/dL) were found to be elevated in 2 of 19 patients. Hematologic malignancies were excluded after bone marrow aspiration smear and trephine biopsy in 14 patients. In 7 of 14 patients (including 2 of 5 confirmed patients), hemophagocytosis with proliferation of histiocytes in bone marrow smears was present (Figure 3).

findings.evidence: Caption: 'Picture of the left forearm of the patient showing ecchymosis.'

panels.rationale: Real-patient clinical photograph of ecchymosis on the left forearm, a classic hemorrhagic manifestation of CCHF, in an article whose primary disease is Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever; however, the patient had triple dengue/CCHF/COVID-19 co-infection, so attribution to CCHF alone carries some uncertainty.
panels.attribution_text: Rahim et al. Dengue Fever, Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever, and COVID-19 Triple Co-infection: Out of the Frying Pan Into the Fire.. Cureus 2022. doi:10.7759/cureus.29028. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Picture of the left forearm of the patient showing ecchymosis.
in_text_mentions: Examination revealed a temperature of 101°F, a pulse of 104 beats per minute, blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg, respiratory rate of 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 92% on room air. He had bruises on both hands and forearms, a bruise on the right flank, and pitting pedal edema limited to the feet (Figure 1, Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Real patient PA chest radiograph showing multifocal bilateral infiltrates, one of the captioned manifestations in this CCHF (triple co-infection) case report. Pulmonary infiltrates are a recognized finding in severe CCHF, though in this case they may also reflect the concurrent dengue/COVID-19 co-infection, so confidence in exclusive CCHF attribution is moderate.

A: Histological slide (bone marrow biopsy) showing macrophages engulfing red blood cells and platelets, which is a manifestation of hemophagocytosis directly related to Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever, as indicated by the caption and arrow. B: Histological slide (bone marrow biopsy) showing a macrophage exhibiting hemophagocytosis, which is a manifestation of the disease, as supported by the figure caption.

in_text_mentions: f symptoms was 5.1 + 3.4 days (range 2–12 days). The median duration between the onset of symptoms and hospital admission was 5.1 + 3.1 days (range 2–12 days). All case-patients had sought care for fever and exanthema with a mean duration of 5.2 + 1.64 days (Figure 2). Eight patients had muscle soreness; 4 patients had diarrhea, and 4 had vomiting, nausea, or both. Three case-patients (5, 6, and 9) underwent bone marrow biopsy; 2 of them, patients 5 and 9, had hemophagocytosis, which fulfilled the criteria for hemophagocytic syndrome (Figure 3). Ferritin serum level was elevated in 7 patients.

A: Clinical photograph of the same laboratory-confirmed autochthonous CCHF patient; caption explicitly attributes ankle erythema 3 days after tick bite. Panel label 'A' present in image. B: Clinical photograph of knee erythema in the same confirmed CCHF case; caption directly supports the finding. Panel label 'B' present. C: Clinical photograph of the necrotic tick-bite site on the back of the confirmed autochthonous CCHF patient; local necrosis at the tick bite is a recognized early CCHF manifestation. Panel label 'C' present.

panels.figure_caption: Retrospectively identified early autochthonous case of Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever in a woman in Spain, 2013. A, B) Erythema in the patient’s ankle (A) and knee (B) 3 days after a tick bite during a leisure walk. C) Necrotic lesion on patient’s back at site of tick bite.
in_text_mentions: experiencing fever and chills. The patient’s general condition worsened the next day (arthromyalgia, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea), and she was admitted to a local hospital. Physical examination revealed erythema (Figure, panels A, B) and a necrotic lesion on the patient’s back in the area of the tick bite (Figure, panel C). Platelet count dropped from 136,000/µL to 17,000/µL in 3 days, accompanied by remarkable leukopenia and neutropenia. Her general condition deteriorated rapidly and she experienced anasarca, gum bleeding, petechiae, and melena; she was transferred to a tertiary hospital.
